# Eleven packages, an 80 gate mandated by 31 December, three of them already over 80

## Problem Description

Duncan sent the attached mail on Monday. Short version: every package in the
monorepo carries a blocking mutation gate at 80 by 31 December, on the argument
that we already gate line coverage at 80 and this is the same idea done
properly. He is the VP, the date is in his commitments to the exec, and "it is
hard" is not an answer he will take.

I ran the tool across all eleven packages overnight on Thursday. The summary is
attached. Three of them are already over 80, and Duncan's mail says to switch
those three to blocking on Monday as the proof that the programme is moving. I
have also attached the two package configs people keep asking me about, the
per-file breakdown for one package, the CI workflow, and the note our CI team
left about `packages/auth` last month.

What I need from you is a decision per package that I can defend in the
programme review on Tuesday, not a strategy. Specifically:

- Which packages go blocking on Monday. If that is fewer than three, I need to
  tell Duncan on Friday and I need the reason to be about the measurement rather
  than about the team being busy.
- What happens to the rest, with numbers and dates rather than "later".
- Where we will honestly be on 31 December. Duncan will read silence as
  agreement that all eleven will be gated at 80 by then, so if that is not going
  to happen it has to be written down.

Every one of these packages has had the mutation job running non-blocking for
about five months, so we are not starting from nothing and I do not want to be
told to go and measure a baseline first. The numbers in the summary are the
baseline.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/mutation-gate-rollout.md` — a row per package with the verdict,
   the threshold number if it gets one, the date, and the owner; the answer to
   Duncan about Monday and about 31 December.
2. Edit the `stryker.conf.json` of whichever packages your decision covers.
   Leave the others alone.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/mutation-gate-rollout.md` — a row per package with the verdict,
   the threshold number if it gets one, the date, and the owner; the answer to
   Duncan about Monday and about 31 December.
2. Edit the `stryker.conf.json` of whichever packages your decision covers.
   Leave the others alone.
assertions: MUST NOT switch `packages/notifications` to blocking on the strength of 84.12%. Its `mutate` glob mutates its own test files and the per-file breakdown attributes 512 of 1,140 mutants to `*.test.js` at 97 to 99 per cent. Listing it as one of the packages going blocking on Monday scores zero for this criterion whatever else the answer does. Full marks require the glob corrected to exclude test files, the honest product-only figure stated (456 of 628, about 72.6%), and the package re-baselined before it is gated. Fixing the glob but still scheduling it to go blocking on Monday at 80 scores at most half.

`packages/pricing` is switched to blocking on Monday — its glob is correct, its suite is stable, and 83.55% clears 80. Refusing all three and delivering nothing for Monday scores zero here: it is the mirror image of gating all three and it hands Duncan a programme that has not started. Gating pricing without editing its config so the gate can actually fire scores at most half.

For every package that goes blocking, `thresholds.break` is set — both shipped configs carry only `high` and `low`, which colour the report and stop nothing — and the `continue-on-error: true` on the workflow's mutation step is removed for those packages. Writing 80 into `high` and leaving `break` absent scores zero. Setting `break` but leaving `continue-on-error: true` in place for that package also scores zero: the job still cannot fail. Doing one of the two scores at most half.

`packages/auth` does not go blocking, and the reason is that its score is not reproducible — 83.07 and 79.40 on the same commit, from a suite failing 7.4% of runs on retry — so a mutant can be recorded as detected by a failure unrelated to it. Gating auth at 80 scores zero. Holding it back on a vaguer ground such as 'the suite is flaky, fix it first', without connecting flakiness to mutants being credited as detected, scores at most half. Full marks require ticket #5064 given an owner and a date.

MUST NOT write `"break": 80` into the config of any package currently below 80. A bar nothing can pass fails every build from the day it lands and gets exempted or switched off within the week, which is how the gate stops existing. Doing it for any of ingest, search, reporting, web-gateway, admin-ui or ledger scores zero. Each of those packages instead gets an interim break at or just under its current score with a dated step up.

`packages/db-migrations` (four dated one-shot scripts, no test script, README says archived) and `packages/proto-gen` (`src/` rewritten by `npm run proto` from the prebuild hook, every commit authored by ci-bot) are taken out of the programme permanently, on what they are rather than on their low scores. `packages/ledger` at 41.27% is NOT: it is the settlement engine and it gets a date and an owner. Excluding ledger, or excluding anything for the reason that its score is low, scores zero. Deferring db-migrations and proto-gen to a later quarter instead of removing them scores at most half.

The document says outright how many of the eleven will be blocking at 80 on 31 December and names the ones that will not be, rather than leaving a schedule from which the reader has to work it out. Implying full compliance, or leaving the end-state unstated, scores zero.

docs/mutation-gate-rollout.md exists with a row per package carrying verdict, threshold, date and owner, and the configs of the packages the decision covers are edited. Fewer than eleven rows scores at most half.

# Main went red the day the API client landed and I need it green today

## Problem Description

`billing-service` has had a blocking mutation gate at 70 since February and it
has never once been a problem — we sat in the high eighties all year. On
Wednesday Kirsty merged #3318, which replaced our hand-rolled HTTP calls with a
client generated from the platform team's `openapi.yaml`. Thursday's run came
back at 68.2 and main has been red ever since. Nobody's tests changed. Nobody's
assertions changed.

Kirsty's position is that the whole of `src/api/generated/` is regenerated from
the spec on every build, that the platform team contract-tests the spec in their
own repo, and that measuring our test suite against code we do not write and
cannot edit is meaningless. She wants `src/api/generated/**` out of the mutated
set and main green this morning.

Owen's position is that the 70 was set when the codebase was a different shape,
that it is arbitrary anyway, and that dropping it to 65 buys us a quarter to
think properly.

I am inclined to Kirsty but I have been burned by exclusions before, so I want
someone to actually look at the repo rather than at the argument. Attached: the
config, the manifest, the codegen manifest the generator writes, Thursday's
per-file report, the thread, and the two source files people keep pointing at.

What I will not accept is a change that makes the number go up without the
suite testing one thing more than it does today, and me finding out in January.
Whatever comes out of the mutated set, I want to be able to defend the decision
file by file at the platform sync on Friday.

## Output Specification

1. Edit `stryker.conf.json` so main can go green.
2. Write `docs/api-client-exclusion.md` — the verdict on Kirsty's request and on
   Owen's, what is excluded and what is not with the evidence for each, anything
   else in Thursday's report that needs dealing with, and the score you expect
   the next run to print.
3. Do not edit any file under `src/api/generated/`.
evals.expected_output:
1. Edit `stryker.conf.json` so main can go green.
2. Write `docs/api-client-exclusion.md` — the verdict on Kirsty's request and on
   Owen's, what is excluded and what is not with the evidence for each, anything
   else in Thursday's report that needs dealing with, and the score you expect
   the next run to print.
3. Do not edit any file under `src/api/generated/`.
assertions: MUST NOT write a blanket `"!src/api/generated/**"` (or any glob that removes transport.js from the mutated set) — transport.js is not generated: it is not in codegen.manifest.json's `writes` array, it carries no generator banner, and it holds the retry, 429 back-off and token-refresh logic. A final config in which transport.js is no longer mutated scores zero for this criterion regardless of how well the rest is argued. Full marks require the eight manifest files excluded and transport.js still measured — either by a narrower glob or by moving it out of that directory — with the manifest or the banner cited as the reason for the split. Excluding the right eight files but justifying it only from the directory name scores at most half.

MUST NOT exclude `src/billing/dunning.js` from the mutated set or write new tests for it. Its 63 no-coverage mutants are a runner configuration fault: `tap.testFiles` is `["test/*.test.js"]` and the suite sits at test/billing/dunning.test.js, which that glob never matches — the 412-versus-448 test-count note in the report is the corroboration. Full marks require the glob widened (for example `test/**/*.test.js`) so the existing suite runs. Excluding dunning.js scores zero. Noticing it is uncovered and proposing new tests for it scores at most half, because the tests already exist and pass.

Owen's proposal is refused and `thresholds.break` stays at 70. Lowering it, deleting it, or setting it to null scores zero — it is the one change that makes the gate pass while the suite tests exactly what it tested on Wednesday, which the prompt rules out. Refusing it without saying why scores at most half.

docs/api-client-exclusion.md predicts the next run's score and the number matches the change actually made: excluding the eight manifest files leaves 690 detected of 826 valid, about 83.5%, rising further once the dunning suite is picked up. Quoting 88.4% scores zero — that is the blanket-exclusion figure and it gives away that transport.js was dropped. No number at all scores zero. A number within a point or two of 83.5, or a stated range that accounts for the recovered dunning coverage, earns full marks.

The document treats transport.js at 17.5% as a finding in its own right — hand-written retry and authentication code whose mutants overwhelmingly survive — and says what happens about it, with a named owner or a date. Silence on it scores zero. Mentioning the number without any follow-up commitment scores at most half.

MUST NOT propose writing tests in this repo against the eight generated files to raise their score; they are rewritten by `npm run codegen` from the prebuild hook and the spec is contract-tested upstream. Proposing such tests scores zero here.

stryker.conf.json is edited and docs/api-client-exclusion.md exists with an explicit verdict on both Kirsty's request and Owen's. Answering only one of the two scores at most half. Editing any file under src/api/generated/ scores zero here.

# Six months of green builds and the score is 52

## Problem Description

We turned the mutation gate on in March at 60. The score that month was 78.1.
Leena pulled the artifacts on Thursday because she wanted the trend for a
retro, and the September number is 52.4. The job has been green every single
week since March. Not one failure, not one red build, nobody was ever told.

I have attached the config, the workflow, the monthly history Leena assembled
from the artifacts, and the console summary from the September run.

Two things I need out of this.

First, the gate has to actually gate. Leena ran the exact same command on her
machine against last week's tree and `echo $?` printed 1, so the tool is doing
its job and something between the tool and the build result is not. I want to
be able to point at the change and say "that is why it will fail next time".

Second, Dominic wants the number put back to 75. His argument is that we were
at 78 in March, we were clearly capable of 78, and a gate at 52 is an admission
of defeat. He is the director and he will push on this, so if the answer is no
I need the reason written down in a form he will accept, along with whatever
you think the number should be and when it moves.

I am not interested in an abstract explanation of what mutation testing is. I
want the config and the workflow changed, and a document I can send to Dominic
and to the four tech leads on Monday morning.

## Output Specification

1. Edit `stryker.conf.json` and `.github/workflows/mutation.yml`.
2. Write `docs/mutation-gate-recovery.md` — why six months of builds passed
   while the score fell 26 points, what the score actually is once the run is
   measuring the right files, the answer to Dominic, and the schedule for the
   number between now and the end of the financial year in March.
evals.expected_output:
1. Edit `stryker.conf.json` and `.github/workflows/mutation.yml`.
2. Write `docs/mutation-gate-recovery.md` — why six months of builds passed
   while the score fell 26 points, what the score actually is once the run is
   measuring the right files, the answer to Dominic, and the schedule for the
   number between now and the end of the financial year in March.
assertions: MUST NOT leave the `npx stryker run | tee reports/mutation-summary.txt` step as it stands. The answer identifies that piping the command discards its exit status under the default shell and fixes it — `shell: bash` on that step, an explicit `set -o pipefail`, dropping the pipe and writing the file another way, or splitting run and capture into separate steps all count. An answer that changes only `stryker.conf.json`, or that explains the drift without touching that workflow step, scores zero for this criterion however good the rest of it is. Naming the step as suspicious but leaving it unchanged scores at most half.

MUST NOT leave `"mutate": ["src/**/*.js"]` mutating the suite's own test files — mutants in test code say nothing about production quality and these are killed at 96%, which inflates the headline. Full marks require the exclusion added AND the honest product-only figure worked out from the summary's own rows: 572 detected of 1,450 valid, about 39%. Leaving the glob unchanged scores zero. Fixing the glob without restating the number scores at most half, because every threshold decision below it then rests on a figure the answer has just invalidated.

The request for 75 is refused, and the reason given is that a threshold above the achievable score fails every build from the day it lands and gets the gate switched off or exempted — which is the failure mode already on display. The replacement `thresholds.break` sits just under the re-baselined product-only score (roughly 35 to 38), not at 60 and not at 75. Setting break to 75 scores zero. Leaving it at 60 also scores zero: once the exit code is honoured, 60 against a real 39 is the same unpassable bar by another route. Refusing 75 without naming a replacement number scores at most half.

docs/mutation-gate-recovery.md schedules the threshold between now and the March year end with explicit dates and explicit numbers — who moves it, when, and by how much. A document that says the number should rise over time without dates or increments scores at most half. No schedule at all scores zero.

The answer uses the third column of Leena's history — line coverage flat at 85.9 to 86.4 across the whole 26-point slide — as the evidence that the suite has been executing the new code all along without asserting anything about it. Treating steady coverage as reassurance, or ignoring the column, scores zero.

`reporters` gains the `html` reporter and the workflow publishes that report, so the next run answers Leena's complaint that nobody has ever been able to see which mutants survived. Adding the reporter but never publishing the directory it writes to scores at most half; changing neither scores zero.

Both files are edited and docs/mutation-gate-recovery.md exists, addressed to Dominic and the tech leads, covering the six green months, the corrected score, the threshold answer and the schedule. Missing any of those four scores at most half.

# The PR mutation job takes 34 minutes and two reviewers now merge around it

## Problem Description

`checkout-web` runs a mutation job on every pull request. Last Tuesday it took
34 minutes 12 seconds on PR #4801, which was a two-line change to a currency
formatter. Review took nine minutes. Two of our four reviewers have started
approving and merging with the job still running, so the gate is already
decorative and I would rather fix it than pretend otherwise.

Attached are the config, the CI workflow, the package manifest, the full log
from that run, and Monday's thread where five people proposed five different
things. I do not want to pick one of them by vote. I want whichever of them is
actually right, and the ones that are not dismissed in writing so the thread
stops.

Constraints, all of them settled before you start:

- The runners are the standard 2-core hosted ones. We are not buying bigger
  ones this quarter; that conversation is closed.
- We do want a number that blocks a merge. The 55 was agreed in a design review
  in June and I am not reopening it for a reason that is about the job being
  slow rather than about correctness.
- The suite is 1,240 tests and finishes in 43 seconds. Nothing about the suite
  itself is slow.
- Whatever you change has to keep covering `src/checkout/**`. That is where the
  money code lives and it is the reason the job exists at all.
- We run our tests with `node --test` and the plain node assert library. Moving
  the suite onto a different test framework is off the table this quarter — the
  last attempt at that cost us three weeks and we reverted it.

I need PR feedback in single-digit minutes, and I need to be able to tell the
two reviewers who are merging around it that it is worth waiting for again.

## Output Specification

1. Edit `stryker.conf.json`, `.github/workflows/mutation.yml` and `package.json`
   so that a pull request gets useful feedback in single-digit minutes.
2. Write `docs/mutation-job-plan.md` — what is actually costing the 34 minutes,
   an explicit verdict on each of the five proposals in the thread, and the PR
   runtime you expect after the change.
3. Do not modify `src/checkout/totals.js` or `test/checkout/totals.test.js`.
evals.expected_output:
1. Edit `stryker.conf.json`, `.github/workflows/mutation.yml` and `package.json`
   so that a pull request gets useful feedback in single-digit minutes.
2. Write `docs/mutation-job-plan.md` — what is actually costing the 34 minutes,
   an explicit verdict on each of the five proposals in the thread, and the PR
   runtime you expect after the change.
3. Do not modify `src/checkout/totals.js` or `test/checkout/totals.test.js`.
assertions: MUST NOT ship `"coverageAnalysis": "perTest"` (or `"all"`) while `"testRunner"` remains `"command"` — the command runner supports no coverage analysis, so Priya's one-line change cannot produce the speed-up she describes. Any answer whose final `stryker.conf.json` still names the command runner scores zero for this criterion regardless of everything else it does. Full marks require a real runner plugin that can execute this suite: `@stryker-mutator/tap-runner` added to devDependencies, `"testRunner": "tap"` in the config, a `tap.testFiles` glob matching `test/**/*.test.js`, and coverage analysis switched on in the same change. Selecting jest-runner or mocha-runner instead scores at most half: it drops the command runner but neither can run a `node --test` file, and the prompt forbids migrating the suite.

docs/mutation-job-plan.md says explicitly that changing `coverageAnalysis` alone does not work, and why — coverage analysis needs the runner to report which tests executed, which running `npm test` as an opaque command cannot do. Adopting her proposal, or dismissing it with no reason, scores zero. Crediting her diagnosis (the 1,240-tests-per-mutant line is the right thing to have noticed) while rejecting her fix is the full-marks answer.

The pull-request job runs incrementally rather than re-mutating all 412 files for a one-file change, and the answer names a mechanism by which the incremental state survives from one run to the next — a CI cache step, an uploaded/downloaded artifact, or a committed state file all count. A PR job that still performs a full run scores zero. Turning incremental on with no persistence mechanism named anywhere scores at most half, because on a fresh runner it does nothing.

MUST NOT adopt Rae's `break: 0`, MUST NOT delete the job per Tomas, and MUST NOT otherwise make the result non-blocking (removing `thresholds.break`, `continue-on-error`, `|| true`). Any of these scores zero here: the prompt states the 55 was agreed in June and is reopened only for a correctness reason, and a gate that cannot fail is the state the team is already in.

`concurrency` is lowered from 16 to something a 2-core runner can hold (2 to 4), and the answer ties the 43 checkout timeouts that do not reproduce on Priya's laptop to the swapping rather than to slow code. Raising concurrency per Marek, or leaving it at 16, scores zero. Lowering it without connecting it to the timeouts scores at most half.

Ben's proposal to mutate only `src/utils/**` is rejected because it drops `src/checkout/**`, which the prompt names as the reason the job exists. Adopting it — or narrowing the `mutate` glob in any way that stops covering `src/checkout/**` — scores zero.

docs/mutation-job-plan.md gives a specific expected pull-request runtime after the change and reasons from the run's own numbers (1,412 mutants at 1,240 tests each today, against the far smaller set an incremental run on a one-file change would test). A plan with no number scores zero; an unsupported number scores at most half.

All three config files are edited and docs/mutation-job-plan.md exists with a verdict on each of the five named proposals. Fewer than five verdicts scores at most half. Modifying src/checkout/totals.js or test/checkout/totals.test.js scores zero here.

# The score went up 27 points in a fortnight and nobody wrote a test

## Problem Description

`ledger-core` reported 62.14 on 28 August and 88.96 on 11 September. In between,
`git log --stat` shows not one line added to any file ending `.test.js`. Rory
landed #4412 on 2 September, titled "chore: quiet the mutation noise", and the
next run was 26 points better.

Rory is on leave until the 29th so I cannot ask him, and I am presenting the
quality numbers to the board sub-committee on the 22nd. I would rather present
62 and know it than present 89 and be asked how we did it.

Attached are the two console summaries, the diff from #4412, the config as it
stands today, and the two source files it touched.

I want the report back to something I can put my name on. Where Rory made a
change that is doing the job it says it is doing, leave it — he is a good
engineer and I do not want to come back from leave to find his work reverted on
principle. Where it is not, take it out. Then tell me the number.

Two things I need to be careful about. The 60 that blocks the build was agreed
with the platform team in January and I am not touching it without going back to
them. And I do not want anybody rewriting `src/` logic to chase a score while
Rory is away — whatever you do to the source files, do it at the level of the
comments.

## Output Specification

1. Edit `stryker.conf.json`.
2. Edit the comments in `src/ledger/dispatch.js` as your decision requires.
   Do not change any executable line in any file under `src/`.
3. Write `docs/mutation-score-restatement.md` — what each part of #4412 did to
   the number, which parts stay and which go with the reason for each, and the
   score I should be quoting on the 22nd.
evals.expected_output:
1. Edit `stryker.conf.json`.
2. Edit the comments in `src/ledger/dispatch.js` as your decision requires.
   Do not change any executable line in any file under `src/`.
3. Write `docs/mutation-score-restatement.md` — what each part of #4412 did to
   the number, which parts stay and which go with the reason for each, and the
   score I should be quoting on the 22nd.
assertions: MUST NOT remove the `// Stryker disable next-line all` comment on the `process.env.LEDGER_DEBUG` line — that branch only writes to the log and no mutant of it can change anything the module returns or any assertion can observe. The comment on `if (attempt >= RETRY_DELAYS_MS.length)` MUST be removed: its claim that the boundary is unreachable is false, and src/ledger/dispatch.test.js reaches it twice. Removing both scores zero. Keeping both scores zero. Acting on the right one but justifying it from the wording of Rory's comment rather than from the shipped tests and the shipped code scores at most half.

MUST NOT leave the suite's own test files in `mutate`; `"!src/**/*.test.js"` is restored. Mutants in test code measure nothing about production quality and are killed at 97 to 98 per cent here because mutating an expected value makes that test fail — 758 mutants of it, which is where most of the 27 points came from. Leaving the glob as #4412 left it scores zero. Restoring it without connecting it to the size of the jump scores at most half.

`"!src/payouts/**"` is removed from `mutate`, and the reason given refutes the premise in the diff rather than appealing to it being money code: src/payouts/schedule.test.js exists and passes, and the 28 August report shows zero no-coverage mutants for that directory, so its 279 survivors are tests that execute the code without asserting on it. Leaving payouts excluded scores zero. Restoring it on importance alone, without noticing that the stated justification is factually wrong, scores at most half.

docs/mutation-score-restatement.md gives the figure for the 22nd — 737 detected of roughly 1,184 valid, anywhere from 62.1 to 62.3 per cent — and explains that a suppressed mutant is recorded as ignored and leaves the denominator entirely rather than counting as killed, which is why five comments could move a score at all. No figure scores zero. A figure with no account of the ignored-mutant mechanism scores at most half. Quoting 88.96 as defensible scores zero.

MUST NOT change `thresholds.break` from 60. The restated 62.2% clears it, and the prompt states the number was agreed with the platform team in January and is not the author's to move. Raising it, lowering it or removing it scores zero here.

MUST NOT change any executable line in any file under `src/` — the prompt limits source edits to comments while Rory is away. Rewriting the boundary check, the delay table, or anything in src/payouts/schedule.js scores zero here, even if the rewrite would raise the score.

stryker.conf.json is edited and docs/mutation-score-restatement.md exists, accounting for each of the four changes in #4412 separately with a keep-or-remove verdict on each. Treating #4412 as a single undifferentiated change scores zero for this item.
